transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-01
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 42 minutes (approx)
Attendees: Taylor Nguyen (Redwood AE), Marcus Li (Redwood SE), Elena Morales (Argosy Cloud Architect), Samir Patel (Argosy Head of Infra), Jia Chen (Argosy Security Lead)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be rough):
Argosy is evaluating Redwood for private VPC deployment. Key constraints: multi-region data residency for EU+US, strict egress/SOC2 audit requirements, they want PrivateLink-style private endpoints or transit gateway peering and IP allowlisting. They have existing NATed egress and want to avoid opening public egress for inference. Next steps: network checklist, hands-on peering workshop, share security docs, runway for a short dedicated trial.

Topics: private endpoints vs peering, transit gateway patterns, NAT/egress, IP ranges, KMS/HSM & key policies, SSO/SCIM, rollout plan and timing.

Transcript body:
[00:00:05] Taylor: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Taylor from Redwood, i'm the AE here. Quick intros, Marcus is our solutions engineer he will run through the networking bits.
[00:00:16] Elena: Hi, Elena here, cloud architect on Argosy infra. We've got Samir and Jia with me.
[00:00:21] Samir: Hey all.
[00:00:23] Jia: Hi.
[00:00:25] Marcus: Great. I'll try to keep the deep stuff pragmatic. We're here to understand your current VPCs and egress posture so we can recommend either PrivateLink, VPC peering, or transit gateway.
[00:00:38] Elena: Right, the main... goal is we can't have any public-facing IPs touching model inference. Our compliance team will not agree to that. We also need EU data residency for a subset of customers.
[00:00:50] Taylor: Totally makes sense. Quick qual question: are you planning a hosted Redwood private tenant inside our VPCs or a private deployment where you manage the control plane?
[00:01:02] Elena: We want a private deployment inside our account, ideally integrated with our KMS and existing IAM. Baseline: no internet-egress for inferencing nodes.
[00:01:14] Marcus: Okay, so that's Private (customer-managed) in our terminology — we can do a VPC-only data plane and a control plane in your account or hybrid where control plane stays with Redwood but data plane is private. Which do you prefer?
[00:01:27] Samir: We'd prefer customer-managed data plane. Control plane could be Redwood if that reduces ops, but we need logs and audit access.
[00:01:36] Jia: Also need KMS integration; key material must stay in our HSM. We have FIPS requirements so can't use vendor-managed keys.
[00:01:45] Marcus: Noted. We have KMS/HSM integrations and support customer-managed keys. There's sometimes small differences in the handshake depending on cloud. Which cloud region footprint are you using?
[00:01:56] Elena: Primary in us-east-1 and eu-west-1, with some latency-sensitive users in ap-southeast-1. We need to ensure inference for EU customers stays in eu-west-1.
[00:02:07] Taylor: So region gating is required; we can route by policy — stick requests to eu models or eu-hosted infra.
[00:02:14] Elena: Yes, and if a request originates in EU we need the data to stay there, including KV cache.
[00:02:20] Marcus: That means you want per-region model pins + KV cache locality and no cross-region replication for those tenant shards. We can enforce that with routing and deployment policies.
[00:02:33] Samir: Network-wise, our infra team prefers Transit Gateway with route policies over dozens of peering connections.
[00:02:41] Marcus: Transit Gateway works fine. For AWS we often recommend TGW if you have many VPCs and a central egress. PrivateLink (interface endpoints) is good for single-VPC integrations or when you want tight IP allowlist without route table changes.
[00:02:54] Jia: Our security team doesn't like exposing many interface endpoints. How does Redwood handle certificate validation and mTLS for endpoints?
[00:03:02] Marcus: We support mutual TLS for service-to-service communication inside the private data plane; our endpoint clients can be configured for mTLS. For interface endpoints we still recommend IP allowlisting and endpoint policies.
[00:03:14] Elena: About egress: right now our VPCs NAT out through central egress; we have strict egress proxies for external calls. If Redwood needs to pull model artifacts from S3 or container registry, how do we get those without direct internet?
[00:03:28] Marcus: Good question. Two common patterns: (1) Allowlist Redwood builder IP ranges and use S3 VPC endpoints with VPC gateway endpoints + endpoint policies, or (2) we can mirror model artifacts into your internal artifact registry (via our artifact sync job) so no outbound is necessary. The latter adds a little lead time for onboarding.
[00:03:46] Samir: We prefer to mirror artifacts to our private registry. Less blast radius.
[00:03:51] Taylor: We'll note that as the recommended pattern. Marcus, can you explain how IP addressing and porting typically look for private clusters?
[00:03:59] Marcus: Sure. The data plane needs a set of ENIs and private IPs for each inference host; we typically ask for a /22 or /21 depending on scale. We'll provide a network checklist with required subnets, route table entries, and security group templates. For TGW you'll point a route to the Redwood attachment. For PrivateLink we provide ENIs in your subnets.
[00:04:20] Elena: If we go PrivateLink, do we need to accept endpoints in each account? We have separate prod, staging, and shared infra accounts.
[00:04:29] Marcus: Yes, you create an interface endpoint per VPC. It's manageable for a few VPCs but at scale TGW reduces administrative overhead.
[00:04:38] Jia: About auditing: we need full request-level logs, who called what model, and token-level cost breakdowns stored for 12 months and immutable for compliance. Can Redwood export to our S3 with write-once rules?
[00:04:52] Taylor: We can export logs to your S3 or to a SIEM via Kinesis or Pub/Sub. For immutability you can apply S3 Object Lock; we provide signing and structured logs in newline-delimited JSON; the storage destination can be your bucket with an inbound bucket policy.
[00:05:06] Samir: What about service endpoints for metrics and healthchecks — do they keep heartbeats to Redwood control plane?
[00:05:12] Marcus: If you choose customer-managed control plane then healthchecks are internal. If control plane is hosted, the data plane still needs to reach Redwood control plane on a set of FQDNs/priv IPs; we have a documented minimal egress list. For complete offline air-gapped on-prem, we have an appliance path but that requires legal and engineering alignment.
[00:05:33] Elena: What's the typical cutover plan? We don't want a big-bang migration.
[00:05:37] Taylor: Most customers do a canary: start with a small subset of traffic or a single model in a staging VPC, verify logs, latency, and cost, then expand. We also support A/B routing and automatic fallback to hosted variants if capacity issues occur.
[00:05:53] Jia: Compliance again — SSO/SCIM integration for our teams? RBAC?
[00:05:58] Marcus: Yes, we support SAML SSO, SCIM for provisioning, and role-based access controls. For Private installations you can map to your IAM roles.
[00:06:06] Elena: On IPs — we have limited public Elastic IPs and don't want to consume them; can Redwood use private NAT only?
[00:06:12] Marcus: Yes. For outbound you can route through your NAT gateway or egress appliances. For inbound private endpoints you don't need Elastic IPs.
[00:06:19] Samir: Let's talk latency: our application requires < 80ms p95 for short prompts in us-east. Is that realistic with a private deployment inside our VPC?
[00:06:28] Marcus: Yes, if the data plane is colocated in us-east and you tune batching to low-latency modes, we can hit that. Model selection and quantization also affects latency. For really low latency we recommend smaller sequence lengths, pinned GPU profiles and local KV cache.
[00:06:42] Taylor: We can run a 48-hour benchmark from a dedicated pool to validate p95 numbers. Do you have a workload sample?
[00:06:50] Elena: We can share a synthetic prompt set.
[00:06:53] Marcus: Great, that'll help us size the /21.
[00:06:58] Jia: A couple of edge questions: how do you handle cross-account IAM? We'll need role assumption for the agent to write to our S3 and register ENIs.
[00:07:08] Marcus: We ask for an IAM role you create with a restricted trust policy for our service principal; we provide fine-grained IAM templates. For some customers we do a read-only role and rely on mirror jobs instead of cross-account writes.
[00:07:20] Samir: And egress IP allowlisting—what's Redwood's SLA on static IP ranges?
[00:07:26] Taylor: For hosted we publish a pool of static egress IP blocks; for private deployments we don't need public egress unless you want artifact downloads. If you choose to allowlist, our published ranges are updated quarterly but we can agree on a long-lived set during onboarding.
[00:07:40] Elena: You mentioned KV cache — is that per-tenant or global? We need tenant isolation.
[00:07:46] Marcus: KV cache is per-deployment and can be pinned per-tenant. We support prefix caching and strict isolation modes.
[00:07:55] Jia: For encryption at rest in the data plane, we need to ensure disk encryption uses our keys.
[00:07:59] Marcus: We support disk encryption with your KMS keys for EBS volumes; for GPUs we also ensure any ephemeral storage is encrypted.
[00:08:08] Taylor: Walk me through concerns that would block a POC. Jia?
[00:08:12] Jia: Primary blockers: KMS/HSM integration (we must use our keys), audit log delivery to our S3 with immutability, and region gating enforcement so EU data never leaves region.
[00:08:24] Taylor: All are typical asks; we'll include those in the checklist. Samir, any operability blockers?
[00:08:29] Samir: IP space planning and how many ENIs we'll need are the main unknowns. Also whether we need to upgrade TGW attachment quotas.
[00:08:37] Marcus: We'll send a sizing doc and a quick script to estimate ENI counts based on concurrent tokens/sec.
[00:08:44] Elena: On timing: can we do a PoC before the end of the quarter?
[00:08:48] Taylor: We can, assuming legal signs off on the standard MSA addendum for private deployments. I'll loop in contracts.
[00:08:55] Jia: For MSA we'll need our DPA and a clause for data locality; is that standard?
[00:09:00] Taylor: Yes, our DPA has region gating options. I'll attach a redline-friendly copy.
[00:09:06] Marcus: Quick note on monitoring: you'll get per-route dashboards and token-level cost breakdowns. We can stream metrics into your Prometheus/Grafana or CloudWatch.
[00:09:16] Samir: Good. If we find a perf regression after a quantized model swap, how are rollbacks handled?
[00:09:22] Marcus: We support canary rollouts and automatic rollback policies tied to evals. You can pin traffic to a previous model version at route time.
[00:09:31] Elena: Anything else we should be aware of for networking?
[00:09:34] Marcus: Two gotchas: (1) overlapping CIDR ranges — we need unique non-overlapping ranges for TGW peering; (2) firewall appliances that do TLS interception can break mTLS unless you exempt the traffic.
[00:09:47] Jia: Good point on TLS interception — we will flag that to our secops.
[00:09:51] Taylor: Ok, quick recap — Taylor will send pricing, network checklist, and MSA/DPA; Marcus will send sizing runbook and peering workshop plan; Argosy will share VPC CIDRs, sample prompts, and confirm KMS needs. We'll aim to reconvene after the checklist is done.
[00:10:09] Samir: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[00:10:13] Elena: Thank you.

(there's a short pause, then off-record side chatter about calendar scheduling)

Meeting notes (manual):

- Logging: export to customer S3 with object lock recommended.
